title: Different, not ranked
hook: these ways aim at different ends: God, awakening, character, calm

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was going deeper in one, and Seneca's warning: everywhere means nowhere. Your line was one well, deep.

A marathon, a swim across a lake, a mountain climb. All three take training, early mornings, sore legs and stubbornness. Someone could line them up and ask which is the best race. It would be a strange question. They aren't three attempts at the same finish line. They end in different places: a tape across a road, a far shore, a summit. On this tour, it's been easy to treat the world's practices as one long race with different running styles, all heading to the same tape. Today asks a plainer question: what is each one actually for?
screen: `A MARATHON, A SWIM, A CLIMB.` → `NOT THE SAME FINISH LINE.` → `WHAT IS EACH ONE FOR?`

segments.voice: Listen to how the practices describe their own ends, in their own words. In Christian prayer and contemplation, the aim is God. Augustine opens his Confessions speaking to God directly: "Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee." The end there isn't a calmer mind, though that may come. It's a relationship, rest in God. In the Buddhist Dhammapada, the end has another name. The verses speak of nirvana, the going out of craving, as the highest happiness. That is awakening, described without a creator God at its center. In the Confucian Analects, the aim is different again: becoming a person of noble character, a junzi, through study, ritual courtesy and care for others. The end is a good human being in a good society. And in modern secular practices, like the mindfulness-based therapy this path met last week, the stated aim is often more modest: calm, attention, a lower chance of falling back into depression. Four ends: God, awakening, character, calm. They overlap at the edges. A Christian may grow calmer, a Buddhist kinder, a therapy patient more thoughtful. But each tradition names its own goal, and the respectful thing is to let it. Saying they're different isn't saying one is better. It's saying each deserves to be understood on its own terms, not folded into someone else's. Comparing aims is description. Ranking them is a different act, and this path doesn't do it.
screen: `GOD: A RESTLESS HEART AT REST.` · `AWAKENING: THE GOING OUT OF CRAVING.` · `CHARACTER: A NOBLE PERSON.` · `CALM: A STEADIER MIND.` · then, large: `DIFFERENT, NOT RANKED.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind your own practice, the one you chose yesterday or any you keep, and ask it gently: what are you for? God, if you pray? Awakening, a better character, a calmer mind, something else entirely? Don't rush to a neat answer; let it be more than one thing if it is, and just listen for what it's reaching toward.
Different. The world's practices aim at different ends, God, awakening, character, calm, and each is understood on its own terms, without a ranking. Today's word.
Your line: different ends. Each deserves to be understood on its own terms. Back tomorrow, same hill.

howItsDone: Traditions describe the aim of practice in their own terms: Christians often speak of union with or rest in God, Buddhists of awakening and nirvana, Confucians of becoming a person of noble character, and secular programs of calm, attention and well-being.

chat.says: Aren't Augustine and the Buddha really after the same thing?
options: Augustine names rest in God; the Dhammapada names nirvana, without a creator God at its center.
Both texts describe rest in a creator God, just using two different words for it.
Both texts say the goal is simply a calmer mind, and nothing more than that.
chat.meaning: Each names its own end: Augustine, a restless heart at rest in God; the Dhammapada, nirvana, the going out of craving. Different, not ranked.
